title: Evaporative Emission Control System Malfunction
shortDescription: Generic EVAP system fault: ECM cannot complete an evaporative system monitor.
fullDescription: P0440 is a generic gross-malfunction code set when the powertrain control module cannot pull or hold vacuum on the EVAP system, indicating a leak, blocked vent, stuck purge, or sensor circuit fault. On most pre-2000 OBD-II vehicles this is the umbrella code; later vehicles set the more specific P0442/P0455/P0456 instead. A loose or non-OEM gas cap is the single most common cause and should always be ruled out first.
safetyImpact: No drivability impact, but the vehicle will fail an OBD-II emissions inspection while the MIL is on.

causes.cause: Loose, missing, or aftermarket fuel cap not sealing
Cracked or disconnected EVAP hose between tank, charcoal canister, and intake
Stuck-open or stuck-closed canister purge valve
Leaking fuel filler neck or O-ring at tank

symptoms: Faint fuel odor near tank or filler

fixSteps.title: Tighten or replace fuel cap
fixSteps.instruction: Remove cap, inspect O-ring for cuts or fuel deposits, reinstall until it clicks 3 times. Clear codes and drive 1-2 cold starts.

fixSteps.title: Run EVAP smoke test
fixSteps.instruction: Connect a low-pressure smoke machine (0.5 psi max) to the service port. Look for smoke at hoses, canister, vent solenoid, and filler neck.

fixSteps.title: Command purge and vent solenoids
fixSteps.instruction: Use bidirectional scan tool to cycle CPV and CVS. Listen for click and verify FTP sensor responds.

fixSteps.title: Replace failed component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace cap, hose, purge or vent solenoid as identified. Use OEM parts. Drive 2 cold-soak drive cycles for monitor to re-run.

faq.q: Can I drive with P0440?
faq.a: Yes. EVAP faults do not affect drivability or engine reliability.

faq.q: Why does it keep coming back after a new gas cap?
faq.a: If the leak is elsewhere (hose or solenoid), a new cap will not clear it. A smoke test is needed.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Incorrect Purge Flow
shortDescription: Purge flow rate does not match commanded value.
fullDescription: P0441 sets when the ECM commands the canister purge valve open and observes either no change in fuel tank pressure (no flow, valve stuck closed or hose blocked) or excessive vacuum (valve stuck open, leaking diaphragm). The test runs during steady-state cruise after the EVAP monitor is enabled.
safetyImpact: No safety impact. May cause minor rough idle if purge valve is stuck open.

causes.cause: Stuck-closed canister purge solenoid (electrical or mechanical)
Stuck-open purge solenoid causing vacuum leak at idle
Plugged or kinked purge line between solenoid and intake

fixSteps.title: Bidirectional purge test
fixSteps.instruction: Command purge solenoid 0% then 100% with engine running. Idle RPM should drop ~50 RPM at 100%. No drop = no flow.

fixSteps.title: Test purge solenoid resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect connector, measure coil resistance. Spec is typically 22-30 ohms at 20C. Out of range = replace.

fixSteps.title: Vacuum test purge valve
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 15 inHg with hand pump. Valve must hold vacuum with no power; release with 12V applied.

fixSteps.title: Replace purge solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace with OEM unit, verify hose routing matches diagram, clear codes, drive cycle.

faq.q: Will P0441 cause stalling?
faq.a: Stuck-open purge can cause rough idle and stall on cold restart, but the valve itself does not damage the engine.

faq.q: How long does the purge solenoid last?
faq.a: Typically 100,000-150,000 miles. Earlier failure suggests contaminated fuel or saturated canister.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Leak Detected (Small Leak)
shortDescription: Small EVAP leak — 0.040 inch (1.0 mm) equivalent orifice.
fullDescription: P0442 indicates a leak equivalent to a 0.040-inch (1.0 mm) orifice in the EVAP system. The ECM seals the system, applies vacuum (or pressure on positive systems like Ford LDP), and watches the FTP sensor. If pressure decays faster than the calibrated threshold, the small-leak code sets. The most common source is the gas cap or filler-neck seal.
safetyImpact: No drivability impact. Will fail OBD-II emissions inspection.

causes.cause: Loose, worn, or non-OEM fuel cap
Cracked filler neck or damaged O-ring
Pinhole leak in EVAP hose or quick-connect
Leaking purge or vent solenoid seat

fixSteps.title: Verify cap and filler neck
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect cap O-ring; replace if cracked or compressed flat. Inspect inside of filler neck for rust or fuel deposits.

fixSteps.title: Smoke test at 0.5 psi
fixSteps.instruction: Plug fresh-air vent, introduce smoke through service port. Inspect with UV light if dye used. Trace smoke to leak.

fixSteps.title: Test FTP sensor
fixSteps.instruction: With key on, FTP should read approximately 2.5V at atmospheric. Apply 5 inH2O — voltage should drop to ~1.5V on most platforms.

fixSteps.title: Repair leak source
fixSteps.instruction: Replace cap, hose, solenoid, or canister as found. Recheck with smoke test before clearing codes.

faq.q: How small is a 0.040 leak?
faq.a: About 1mm — the diameter of a thumbtack pinhole.

faq.q: Why does it take days to come back?
faq.a: EVAP monitor only runs once per cold soak under specific fuel-level and ambient conditions.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Purge Control Valve Circuit
shortDescription: Electrical fault in purge solenoid control circuit.
fullDescription: P0443 sets when the ECM detects an open or short on the canister purge solenoid driver circuit. Unlike flow codes (P0441), this is purely electrical: the ECM monitors current through the solenoid coil and compares to expected. The companion specific codes (P0444 open, P0445 short) appear on most modern platforms.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Chafed wiring shorting to ground or power

fixSteps.title: Measure purge solenoid coil
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect connector. Measure resistance — should be 22-30 ohms. Open or shorted = replace solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Check power feed
fixSteps.instruction: Key on, backprobe power side of connector. Should see battery voltage.

fixSteps.title: Check driver circuit
fixSteps.instruction: Reconnect, command 50% duty cycle. Backprobe driver wire — should pulse between 0V and 12V.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid or repair wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Repair chafed wire with solder and heat shrink, or replace solenoid. Clear codes.

faq.q: Difference between P0441 and P0443?
faq.a: P0441 is flow-rate (mechanical or hose), P0443 is purely electrical circuit.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Vent Control Circuit
shortDescription: Vent solenoid (CVS) circuit malfunction.
fullDescription: P0446 sets when the canister vent solenoid circuit fails its rationality test. The CVS is normally open, allowing the charcoal canister to breathe atmosphere; the ECM closes it to seal the EVAP system for leak testing. P0446 indicates an electrical fault, blocked vent path, or stuck solenoid. Common on GM trucks where the CVS is mounted near the rear axle and floods or rusts.
safetyImpact: Possible inability to refuel without clicking off (sealed tank).

causes.cause: Water or mud contamination of CVS (especially GM trucks)

symptoms: Pump shuts off repeatedly when refueling
Possible P0455 or P0442 also set

fixSteps.title: Locate and inspect CVS
fixSteps.instruction: Find solenoid (typically near canister, often on frame rail). Inspect for water, mud, rust on connector.

fixSteps.title: Measure coil resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect, measure across pins. Spec ~25 ohms typical. Replace if open or shorted.

fixSteps.title: Functional test
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 12V — solenoid should click and seal. Blow through both ports — sealed when energized, open when off.

fixSteps.title: Replace and protect connector
fixSteps.instruction: Install OEM solenoid, apply dielectric grease, ensure drain holes are clear. Clear codes.

faq.q: Why is this so common on GM trucks?
faq.a: The CVS is exposed under the truck near the canister — water, salt, and mud pack the connector.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Vent Valve/Solenoid Circuit
shortDescription: CVS circuit open or shorted (electrical only).
fullDescription: P0449 reports an open or short on the canister vent solenoid driver circuit. Distinct from P0446 (rationality / flow), P0449 fires immediately on key-on if the ECM cannot detect coil current. Frequently caused by corroded connector pins or chafed harness where it transitions from frame to canister.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Open ECM ground or driver fault

fixSteps.title: Inspect connector
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect CVS connector — look for green corrosion or trapped water. Clean with electrical contact cleaner.

fixSteps.title: Coil resistance test
fixSteps.instruction: Measure across solenoid pins. Replace solenoid if outside 20-30 ohm range.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test wiring
fixSteps.instruction: With ECM commanding solenoid, wiggle harness while watching live data. Intermittent open = chafed wire.

fixSteps.title: Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid and/or repair harness. Use weatherpack-grade connector and heat shrink.

faq.q: Can a bad CVS prevent fueling?
faq.a: Yes — if stuck closed, the tank cannot vent and the pump shuts off.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
shortDescription: FTP sensor signal noisy or out of expected range.
fullDescription: P0451 sets when the fuel tank pressure (FTP) sensor signal is rational but noisy, drifts, or fails to track expected pressure changes during refueling and key-off cool down. Often appears alongside P0455 because the ECM cannot trust the leak test. Usually a failing FTP sensor; sometimes a small intermittent leak that creates erratic readings.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: FTP sensor internal drift or wear
Saturated or contaminated FTP diaphragm (fuel intrusion)

symptoms: Inconsistent fuel gauge on some platforms

fixSteps.title: Read FTP voltage at key-on
fixSteps.instruction: FTP should be ~2.5V at atmosphere. Less than 0.5V or more than 4.5V = circuit fault.

fixSteps.title: Apply controlled vacuum
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 5 inH2O vacuum to FTP — voltage should drop ~1V smoothly with no jitter.

fixSteps.title: Verify reference and ground
fixSteps.instruction: Backprobe — 5V reference present, signal ground less than 0.1V vs battery ground.

fixSteps.title: Replace FTP sensor
fixSteps.instruction: On most vehicles requires dropping fuel tank or accessing through rear seat. Use OEM only — aftermarket sensors often calibrate poorly.

faq.q: Where is the FTP sensor?
faq.a: Usually on top of the fuel tank or built into the fuel-pump module.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Pressure Sensor Low Input
shortDescription: FTP signal voltage stuck low.
fullDescription: P0452 sets when the fuel tank pressure sensor signal is below the low threshold (typically 0.1-0.5V) for several seconds. Indicates a shorted-to-ground signal, failed sensor, or excessive negative tank pressure. Verify that no one recently fueled while the engine was running — that can momentarily set this code on some platforms.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: FTP signal wire shorted to ground
Plugged tank vent causing real vacuum buildup

symptoms: Possible P0451 or P0455 companion codes

fixSteps.title: Disconnect FTP
fixSteps.instruction: With sensor disconnected, key on — signal should rise to ~5V (open circuit). If still 0V, wire is shorted to ground.

fixSteps.title: Verify 5V ref at sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Should read 5V key-on. If 0V, check ECM and wiring for that reference circuit.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: If reference and ground are good but voltage stays low with sensor connected, replace sensor.

fixSteps.title: Check for tank vacuum
fixSteps.instruction: Loosen fuel cap with key off — listen for inrush of air. Strong vacuum indicates blocked vent line.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Pressure Sensor High Input
shortDescription: FTP signal voltage stuck high.
fullDescription: P0453 sets when the FTP sensor signal exceeds the high threshold (typically 4.5V) for several seconds. Most often the result of an open signal wire or open ground at the sensor. Less commonly the tank is over-pressurized due to a seized vent solenoid combined with thermal expansion of fuel.
safetyImpact: No safety impact under normal use; tank over-pressure can cause filler-neck spit-back when cap is removed.

causes.cause: Stuck-closed vent solenoid causing real over-pressure

symptoms: Possible loud whoosh on cap removal (if real over-pressure)

fixSteps.title: Backprobe signal at sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Key on, engine off — voltage should be ~2.5V. If 5V with sensor connected, sensor or ground is open.

fixSteps.title: Jumper signal to ground
fixSteps.instruction: Briefly jumper signal pin to sensor ground at the harness side — voltage should drop to 0V at scan tool. If yes, ECM and wiring OK; replace sensor.

fixSteps.title: Verify ground at sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Key on, measure sensor ground vs battery negative. Less than 0.1V drop. If higher, repair ground.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace with OEM. Re-test before reinstalling fuel module.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Leak Detected (Large Leak)
shortDescription: Large EVAP leak — 0.080 inch (2.0 mm) equivalent.
fullDescription: P0455 indicates a large gross leak — equivalent to a 0.080-inch (2 mm) hole, or a completely missing/loose gas cap. The ECM seals the EVAP system and watches for any vacuum or pressure change; on a gross leak it sees essentially none. Almost always recoverable with cap inspection and a smoke test.
safetyImpact: No safety impact. Strong fuel odor possible.

causes.cause: Disconnected EVAP hose at canister or purge
Cracked filler neck or split hose

fixSteps.title: Cap and visual
fixSteps.instruction: Re-seat cap, listen for clicks. Inspect all visible EVAP hoses on top of tank, at canister, and at purge valve.

fixSteps.title: Smoke test
fixSteps.instruction: Apply low-pressure smoke at service port. Large leak will show smoke immediately at the source.

fixSteps.title: Inspect filler neck
fixSteps.instruction: Common rust-out point on older vehicles — remove inner fender liner and look at filler-to-tank junction.

fixSteps.title: Repair source
fixSteps.instruction: Replace cap, hose, neck, or solenoid. Re-smoke before clearing codes.

faq.q: Is it safe to drive?
faq.a: Yes, but you may smell raw fuel — keep windows cracked.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Leak Detected (Very Small Leak)
shortDescription: Very small EVAP leak — 0.020 inch (0.5 mm).
fullDescription: P0456 indicates a tiny leak (0.020 in / 0.5 mm) that took multiple drive cycles to confirm. Often the hardest EVAP code to chase. Causes are usually a marginal fuel-cap seal, a hairline crack in plastic hardware, or a slightly leaking valve seat. A meticulous smoke test with the system pressurized for 5+ minutes is essential.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Hairline crack in EVAP hose, often near heat
Tiny seat leak in purge or vent solenoid

symptoms: MIL on after several drive cycles

fixSteps.title: Replace cap as a baseline
fixSteps.instruction: Even if cap looks fine, install OEM new cap as cheap insurance.

fixSteps.title: Pressurized smoke test, 5 minutes
fixSteps.instruction: Smoke at 0.5 psi for at least 5 minutes — small leaks need time. Use UV dye for confirmation.

fixSteps.title: Pinch-test branches
fixSteps.instruction: While smoking, sequentially pinch off canister vent, purge, and tank lines to isolate which side leaks.

fixSteps.title: Replace identified part
fixSteps.instruction: Repair or replace exact source. Avoid generic 'replace charcoal canister' guesses.

faq.q: Why is P0456 so hard to find?
faq.a: The leak orifice is the size of a sewing needle — only patient smoke testing reveals it.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Leak Detected (Fuel Cap Loose/Off)
shortDescription: EVAP leak specifically attributed to fuel cap.
fullDescription: P0457 is a code dedicated to gross leaks consistent with a missing or loose fuel cap. Some platforms (Ford, GM) display 'Check Fuel Cap' on the cluster when this sets. Differs from P0455 in that the diagnostic specifically detected the leak signature pattern that matches an open cap rather than a hose disconnection.
safetyImpact: No safety impact. Possible fuel splash if cap is missing.

causes.cause: Cap not clicked all the way down

fixSteps.title: Tighten until 3 clicks
fixSteps.instruction: Remove and reinstall cap until ratchet has clicked at least 3 times.

fixSteps.title: Inspect O-ring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for cuts, swelling, or fuel deposits. Replace cap if worn.

fixSteps.title: Inspect filler neck threads
fixSteps.instruction: Look down filler neck — threads should be undamaged. Wire-brush any rust.

fixSteps.title: Drive cycle and clear
fixSteps.instruction: Many vehicles auto-clear after 2-3 successful EVAP monitors.

faq.q: Will it clear on its own?
faq.a: Yes — most vehicles auto-clear after a few drive cycles with a tight cap.

title: Evaporative Emission System Purge Control Valve Circuit Low
shortDescription: Purge solenoid driver circuit shorted to ground.
fullDescription: P0458 sets when the ECM detects the canister purge solenoid driver pulled to ground when it should be open. Either the solenoid coil is shorted or the wire from solenoid to ECM is grounded. Quick test: unplug solenoid, key on — code should change to high/open if wiring is fine.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

fixSteps.title: Coil resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Measure across solenoid pins. Less than 15 ohms = shorted, replace.

fixSteps.title: Wiring short test
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect solenoid AND ECM connector for that circuit. Measure driver wire to chassis ground — should be infinite.

fixSteps.title: Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid or repair grounded wire with heat-shrink splice.

title: Evaporative Emission System Purge Control Valve Circuit High
shortDescription: Purge solenoid driver circuit shorted to power or open.
fullDescription: P0459 indicates the ECM sees the purge solenoid driver pulled high (battery voltage) when it should be commanded low, or the circuit is open. Indicates either an open coil, an open driver wire, or a short to power.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Short to battery on driver wire

fixSteps.title: Verify coil
fixSteps.instruction: Measure resistance — open = replace solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Continuity ECM-to-solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: With both ends disconnected, check continuity of driver wire — should be near 0 ohms.

fixSteps.title: Short-to-power check
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect both ends, key on, measure driver wire to ground — should be 0V.

fixSteps.title: Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid or repair wiring. Clear code.

title: Fuel Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: Fuel level sensor reading is implausible.
fullDescription: P0461 sets when the fuel level sensor signal does not change in a manner consistent with fuel consumption — for example, level stays constant for many miles, or jumps unrealistically. Required because the EVAP monitor uses fuel level to decide when to run leak tests; an unreliable sensor blocks all EVAP diagnostics.
safetyImpact: Inaccurate fuel gauge can lead to running out of fuel.

causes.cause: Worn fuel level sender wiper or float (most common after 100k mi)
Sulfur deposits on sender resistance card
Wiring intermittent at fuel pump connector

fixSteps.title: Watch fuel level PID
fixSteps.instruction: Drive while watching fuel level percentage on scan tool — should change smoothly with consumption.

fixSteps.title: Bench test sender
fixSteps.instruction: After dropping tank or accessing through service hole, sweep float manually — resistance must change smoothly across full range.

fixSteps.title: Replace sender or pump module
fixSteps.instruction: Most modern senders are integral to fuel pump module — replace assembly. Use OEM for accurate calibration.

faq.q: Top-tier gas help?
faq.a: Yes — sulfur deposits on the sender are reduced by using fuels with proper detergents.

title: Fuel Level Sensor Circuit High
shortDescription: Fuel level sensor signal stuck high.
fullDescription: P0463 indicates the fuel level signal is above the maximum threshold (open circuit). Most commonly the sender's wiper has fallen off the resistance card or the signal wire is open. Also caused by a corroded fuel-pump module connector — the typical fault on long-running vehicles.
safetyImpact: Possible fuel gauge reading full when nearly empty — running out of fuel risk.

causes.cause: Open signal wire to instrument cluster / ECM

symptoms: Fuel gauge reads full or pegged high

fixSteps.title: Inspect pump connector
fixSteps.instruction: Access fuel pump connector (under rear seat or in trunk). Inspect for melted pins or green corrosion.

fixSteps.title: Short-test signal
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect connector at pump, jumper signal pin to ground — gauge should read empty. If yes, sender is open.

fixSteps.title: Replace sender or pigtail
fixSteps.instruction: Replace fuel pump module if integral, or replace harness pigtail if connector is the only damage.

title: Exhaust Pressure Sensor Malfunction
shortDescription: Exhaust back-pressure sensor circuit fault.
fullDescription: P0470 sets on diesel and some turbo gas vehicles when the exhaust pressure sensor signal is implausible or out of range. Used for EGR and DPF management. Most often the sensor's tube to the exhaust is plugged with soot, or the sensor itself has failed from heat exposure.
safetyImpact: May trigger reduced power mode on diesels with active DPF regeneration limits.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor tube
fixSteps.instruction: Remove sensor pickup tube from exhaust — soot blockage is extremely common. Clean with brass brush and brake cleaner.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Compare static voltage at key-on (atmospheric) to spec. Apply small pressure and observe linear response.

fixSteps.title: Replace if failed
fixSteps.instruction: Use OEM sensor — high-temp aftermarket units fail prematurely. Apply anti-seize on threads.

faq.q: Common on which vehicles?
faq.a: Ford 6.0 / 6.4 Power Stroke, GM Duramax, VW TDI, Cummins.

title: Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit
shortDescription: Primary cooling fan relay or driver circuit fault.
fullDescription: P0480 sets when the ECM detects an open or short on the primary cooling fan control circuit. Listed under emissions because cooling-fan failure can cause overheating that affects catalyst efficiency and emissions. Pay attention — this code can precede a no-warning overheat.
safetyImpact: Engine overheating risk if fan does not run during low-speed operation.
symptoms: Engine temperature climbs at idle / stop
AC may stop cooling at idle
Fan does not run after engine off

fixSteps.title: Inspect fuse and relay
fixSteps.instruction: Pull fan fuse, inspect. Swap fan relay with identical relay and retest.

fixSteps.title: Direct-power fan motor
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 12V and ground directly to fan motor — must spin smoothly with no growl.

fixSteps.title: Command fan via scan tool
fixSteps.instruction: Use bidirectional control to turn fan on. Verify relay clicks and motor runs.

fixSteps.title: Replace failed component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace fan motor, relay, or repair wiring. Verify fan runs at proper coolant temp threshold.

faq.q: Drive with this code?
faq.a: Only short trips with continuous airflow — never sit idling. Overheat damage is expensive.

title: Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit
shortDescription: Secondary cooling fan relay or driver circuit fault.
fullDescription: P0481 covers the secondary (high-speed or AC condenser) cooling fan circuit. Same diagnostic flow as P0480 but on the secondary fan. On dual-fan setups, one fan handles low-demand cooling and the other engages for AC or high-load. Failure may cause AC degradation before engine overheating.
safetyImpact: AC may not cool at idle; engine may overheat under high load.
symptoms: Coolant temperature creeps up under load

fixSteps.title: Test relay and fuse
fixSteps.instruction: Swap relay with known good. Inspect fuse.

fixSteps.title: Direct-power fan
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 12V to fan-2 — must spin smoothly.

fixSteps.title: Bidirectional command
fixSteps.instruction: Command fan-2 high via scan tool. Confirm operation.

fixSteps.title: Replace component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace failed fan, relay, or repair wiring.

title: Cooling Fan Rationality Check
shortDescription: Fan output does not match commanded state.
fullDescription: P0483 fires when the ECM commands the cooling fan(s) on but the feedback (current draw, RPM signal on PWM fans, or thermostat housing temperature behavior) does not match. Common with electric/PWM fans where the controller reports incorrect status.
safetyImpact: Possible overheat under high load.

causes.cause: Failed fan controller / driver module (PWM fans)
Wiring fault between ECM and controller

fixSteps.title: Verify ECT signal
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm coolant temp PID is plausible and stable.

fixSteps.title: Watch fan duty cycle
fixSteps.instruction: On scan tool, observe commanded fan duty vs actual fan PWM signal at controller. Mismatch = controller fault.

fixSteps.title: Inspect fan controller
fixSteps.instruction: Many modern vehicles use a separate fan-control module attached to the shroud. Check for heat damage.

fixSteps.title: Replace controller or fan assembly
fixSteps.instruction: Most fan controllers come integrated with the fan shroud — replace as assembly.

title: Evaporative Emission System High Purge Flow
shortDescription: Excessive purge flow — vacuum leak through purge solenoid.
fullDescription: P0496 sets when the ECM observes too much fuel tank vacuum during purge testing. Indicates the canister purge valve is leaking when commanded closed, providing a steady vacuum leak to the intake manifold. Common cause of rough idle that may not throw a vacuum leak code immediately.
safetyImpact: Possible stalling at idle.

causes.cause: Cracked purge hose downstream of valve (constant vacuum)

fixSteps.title: Pinch purge hose at idle
fixSteps.instruction: Pinch purge hose between intake and solenoid — if rough idle smooths, purge is leaking.

fixSteps.title: Vacuum-test valve
fixSteps.instruction: Remove valve, apply 15 inHg with no power — must hold. Energize 12V — must release.

fixSteps.title: Replace valve
fixSteps.instruction: Install OEM purge solenoid. Inspect canister for liquid fuel (saturation can damage the new valve).

title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation Flow Insufficient
shortDescription: EGR flow lower than commanded.
fullDescription: P0401 sets when the ECM commands the EGR valve open and the differential pressure sensor (DPFE) or MAP shows less flow than expected. Typically caused by carbon buildup blocking EGR passages — extremely common on Ford 4.6 and on direct-injection engines after 80,000 miles.
safetyImpact: May increase NOx emissions, may cause pinging under load.

causes.cause: Carbon-clogged EGR passages or valve seat
Cracked or disconnected EGR vacuum hose (older systems)

fixSteps.title: Command EGR open
fixSteps.instruction: Use bidirectional command — RPM should drop ~150 RPM at hot idle. No drop = no flow.

fixSteps.title: Remove and inspect valve
fixSteps.instruction: Pull EGR valve, look at pintle and seat. Heavy carbon = clean with chemical and brass brush.

fixSteps.title: Inspect EGR passages
fixSteps.instruction: Probe the inlet and outlet ports — if hard carbon plug present, intake manifold may need to be removed for full clean.

fixSteps.title: Test DPFE (if equipped)
fixSteps.instruction: Compare DPFE voltage at idle vs high RPM. Replace DPFE if non-linear or stuck.

faq.q: Can I bypass EGR?
faq.a: No — illegal on most public roads, and reduces detonation margin under load.

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)
shortDescription: Bank 1 catalyst inefficient — downstream O2 mirroring upstream.
fullDescription: P0420 sets when the rear (post-cat) O2 sensor on Bank 1 oscillates similarly to the front sensor, indicating the catalyst is not storing/releasing oxygen — i.e., reduced efficiency. Causes range from a worn catalyst to upstream issues like a leaky exhaust, bad upstream O2 sensor, or rich/lean conditions damaging the brick.
safetyImpact: No drivability impact, but the catalyst may be near complete failure. Will fail emissions.

causes.cause: Aged catalytic converter (loss of precious-metal coating)
Exhaust leak before or between O2 sensors
Aged or contaminated rear O2 sensor
Engine running rich (failed injector, leaking fuel pressure regulator)
Misfire damaging the cat (look for P030x history)
Coolant or oil consumption coating the catalyst

symptoms: Rare power loss if cat is internally collapsing

fixSteps.title: Compare O2 traces
fixSteps.instruction: View both Bank-1 sensors live. Front should oscillate 0.1-0.9V; rear should be lazy at ~0.6-0.8V. If rear mirrors front = cat low.

fixSteps.title: Smoke-test exhaust
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm no exhaust leaks before catalyst — even pinhole leaks throw P0420.

fixSteps.title: Cat-temperature check
fixSteps.instruction: After warm-up, IR-temp inlet vs outlet of cat. Outlet should be 50-100F hotter on a healthy cat.

fixSteps.title: Replace catalyst
fixSteps.instruction: Use OEM-spec or CARB-certified aftermarket. Replace upstream O2 if 100k+ miles. Address upstream root cause first or new cat will fail again.

faq.q: Will an O2 sensor fix it?
faq.a: Sometimes — a lazy rear O2 mimics a bad cat. Test before replacing the converter.

faq.q: Is the cat covered under warranty?
faq.a: Federal emissions warranty covers the catalyst for 8 years / 80,000 miles in the US.

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Bank 2 catalyst inefficient.
fullDescription: P0430 is the Bank 2 counterpart to P0420 — the rear O2 on Bank 2 is mirroring the front, indicating the catalyst is not properly storing/releasing oxygen. Diagnostic flow is identical to P0420 but applies to the bank that does not include cylinder #1.
safetyImpact: No drivability impact. Fails emissions.

causes.cause: Bank 2 running rich (injector or fuel-trim issue)

fixSteps.title: Compare Bank 2 O2 traces
fixSteps.instruction: Same procedure as P0420 but on Bank 2. Identify which bank cylinder #1 is on first — Bank 2 is the other side.

fixSteps.title: Inspect for exhaust leaks
fixSteps.instruction: Smoke or audible test on Bank 2 manifold and pre-cat pipe.

fixSteps.title: Replace catalyst or O2
fixSteps.instruction: Replace converter or rear O2 sensor as confirmed. Address fuel-trim issues first.

title: Secondary Air Injection System Incorrect Flow Detected
shortDescription: Secondary air injection (SAI) flow incorrect during cold start.
fullDescription: P0411 sets when the ECM commands the SAI pump on at cold start and the upstream O2 sensors do not register the expected lean spike. Indicates the secondary air pump, check valves, or piping are not delivering air to the exhaust during the first ~60 seconds after cold start. Common on BMW, VW, Audi after 80,000 miles.
safetyImpact: Cold-start emissions affected; will fail emissions in many regions.

causes.cause: Failed SAI pump (water-damaged or worn brushes)
Stuck check valve (carbon-fused open or closed)

symptoms: Loud pump noise at cold start

fixSteps.title: Listen at cold start
fixSteps.instruction: Within 30 seconds of cold start, listen for SAI pump whirring near the air filter or under fender. No noise = pump or relay.

fixSteps.title: Power test pump
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 12V to pump connector — must run smoothly with no growl or seized rotor.

fixSteps.title: Check valve test
fixSteps.instruction: Remove check valve, apply pressure from pump side — must allow air through; from exhaust side — must block. Replace if either fails.

fixSteps.title: Replace failed components
fixSteps.instruction: Use OEM. Pump location often hidden behind fender liner.

faq.q: Can I bypass the SAI system?
faq.a: No — emissions equipment removal is illegal under federal law in the US.

title: Warm-Up Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Bank 2 close-coupled (warm-up) catalyst inefficient.
fullDescription: P0431 applies to the warm-up (close-coupled) catalyst on Bank 2 in vehicles equipped with a small pre-cat near the manifold. Diagnostic concept matches P0420/P0430 but specific to the warm-up converter, which sees the highest temperatures and tends to fail first.
safetyImpact: Fails emissions.

fixSteps.title: Compare upstream/mid O2 sensors on Bank 2
fixSteps.instruction: Mid-bed (between warm-up cat and main cat) O2 should be lazy on a healthy cat.

fixSteps.title: Identify and address engine-side root cause
fixSteps.instruction: Resolve any rich/misfire/oil-burning issue first.

fixSteps.title: Replace warm-up cat
fixSteps.instruction: Often integrated with manifold — costly job. Use OEM if possible.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Purge Control Valve Circuit Open
shortDescription: Open circuit detected on purge solenoid.
fullDescription: P0444 reports an open circuit on the purge valve driver — either an open coil winding, broken wire, or pushed-back terminal in the connector. ECM detects no current flow when commanding the solenoid. Often accompanies P0443 on platforms that store both.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Broken wire from chafing or rodent damage

fixSteps.title: Inspect connector pins
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect, look at female terminals — pushed back is common. Re-tension with pick.

fixSteps.title: Coil resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Open circuit = replace solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Continuity ECM-side
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect ECM connector for that pin and test continuity to solenoid harness end.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Purge Control Valve Circuit Shorted
shortDescription: Short circuit on purge solenoid driver.
fullDescription: P0445 indicates a short on the purge solenoid driver circuit. Either the coil is internally shorted (low resistance) or the driver wire is touching power or ground. The ECM detects excessive current and disables the driver to protect itself.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

causes.cause: Driver wire grounded against engine or body

symptoms: Possible blown ECM driver if recurring

fixSteps.title: Coil resistance test
fixSteps.instruction: Less than 15 ohms typically = shorted, replace solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Wiring inspection
fixSteps.instruction: With both ends disconnected, measure driver wire to chassis ground — should be infinite. Less than 1 ohm = grounded wire.

fixSteps.title: Repair and replace
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid; repair grounded wire with proper insulation.

title: Evaporative Emission Control System Vent Control Circuit Shorted
shortDescription: Vent solenoid driver shorted.
fullDescription: P0448 sets on a short on the canister vent solenoid driver — the ECM sees excessive current to ground and disables the driver. Common after off-road use that floods the CVS connector with mud or water.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

fixSteps.title: Inspect connector
fixSteps.instruction: Check for water intrusion or corrosion at CVS connector under vehicle.

fixSteps.title: Coil short test
fixSteps.instruction: Resistance under 15 ohms = replace solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Wiring short-to-ground
fixSteps.instruction: Both ends disconnected, driver wire to chassis = should be infinite.

title: Evaporative Emission System Low Purge Flow
shortDescription: Purge flow below expected — restriction or stuck-closed valve.
fullDescription: P0497 indicates the ECM commanded purge but observed insufficient flow. Differs from P0496 (high flow) — P0497 is restricted/blocked. Common causes are a saturated charcoal canister, plugged purge tube, or a stuck-closed solenoid.
safetyImpact: No safety impact.

fixSteps.title: Bidirectional purge test
fixSteps.instruction: 100% command should drop idle ~50 RPM. No drop = no flow.

fixSteps.title: Solenoid bench test
fixSteps.instruction: Apply 12V — must open. Apply vacuum — must hold then release.

fixSteps.title: Inspect canister
fixSteps.instruction: Liquid fuel saturation = replace canister and find why fuel got into it (overfilling, faulty rollover valve).

fixSteps.title: Replace failed component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid, hose, or canister as needed.
